text:
The lighthouse at Corran Point was built of grey granite quarried from the hills behind the village, and for most of its life it was kept by a single family who passed the duty from parent to child.

Each evening the keeper climbed one hundred and twelve steps to the lamp room, trimmed the wicks, polished the brass, and wrote the weather into a leather ledger that still survives in the harbour office.

The ledger records storms in plain words. In the winter of the great gale the keeper wrote that the sea came over the lower gallery three times in one night and that the glass of the seaward window cracked but held.

Supplies came by boat once a fortnight when the weather allowed it. Flour, lamp oil, candles, salted fish and letters arrived together, and the keeper's children learned to read from the newspapers wrapped around the parcels.

When the light was converted to electricity the family stayed on as caretakers. They painted the tower every third summer, repaired the slate roof of the cottage, and kept a small garden of potatoes and kale behind a stone wall.

Visitors often asked whether the work was lonely. The last keeper answered that the light was never lonely, because every ship that passed was a conversation, even if neither side could hear the other speak.

The tower was finally automated in the spring of a dry year. The ledger, the brass lamp and a painted sign reading Corran Point were carried down the steps and placed in the harbour office, where they remain on display.

Today the cottage is used by walkers as a shelter. A visitors' book sits on the table by the window, and many of the entries describe the same thing the keepers wrote about: the long beam turning slowly over dark water.

The town of Hollin Lock grew up around a flight of seven locks that lifted the canal over a low ridge of chalk. Before the canal arrived there were only a mill, a chapel and a handful of cottages along the stream.

Boats carried coal north and brought back grain, timber and bricks. The lock keepers kept a tally of every boat in a register, noting the cargo, the owner's name and the time it took to pass through all seven chambers.

Working the locks was slow. A loaded boat needed nearly an hour to climb the flight, so an inn opened beside the top lock where crews could eat, rest their horses and trade news from the towns along the route.

The inn kept a long table near the fire for boat crews and a smaller room for travellers who arrived by coach. Its cellar held barrels of cider pressed from the orchards that grew on the south side of the ridge.

Floods were the great danger. In a wet autumn the stream rose over its banks, filled the lower pound and pushed a moored boat against the gates of the fourth lock until the timber split along its length.

Repairs took the whole winter. Carpenters shaped new gates from oak felled in the estate woods, and blacksmiths forged the iron straps and paddles by the light of a forge set up on the towpath beside the damaged lock.

Trade on the canal declined once the railway reached the valley. The locks fell quiet, the inn became a farmhouse, and reeds grew across the lower pounds until a volunteer society began clearing them many years later.

The society now opens the flight on summer weekends. Children help push the balance beams, and an old register from the lock keeper's hut is kept in a glass case so visitors can read the names of the boats.

The glassworks at Fennick stood beside a fast river that turned the wheel of its grinding mill. Sand came from the dunes to the west, and the furnaces burned wood until coal arrived by cart from the valley pits.

Inside the cone the heat was so great that the gatherers worked in short turns. Each gatherer dipped an iron pipe into the pot, turned it slowly to collect a glowing ball of glass, and passed it to the blower at the bench.

The blowers shaped bottles, jars and window panes. A skilled blower could make several hundred bottles in a day, and the best of them were known by the small marks they pressed into the base of every piece.

Window glass was made by blowing a large bubble, cutting it open and spinning it into a flat disc. The thick centre of each disc was sold cheaply for cottage windows, which is why so many old panes have a round knot of glass.

Children worked at the glassworks too, carrying finished pieces to the annealing oven where they cooled slowly overnight. Without the slow cooling the glass would crack, and a whole day of work could be lost by morning.

The works closed after a fire spread from the packing shed into the timber roof of the cone. Nobody was hurt, but the furnace pots cracked as they cooled and the owners decided that rebuilding would cost too much.

Fragments of green and brown glass still wash out of the riverbank after heavy rain. Local collectors gather them and sort them by colour, and a small museum in the old school displays the finest bottles with their makers' marks.
